We find that the star formation rate and mass relation exhibits a sharp decline at higher masses, which we attribute to the rapid growth of massive galaxies through mergers. We also examine the connection between the star formation rate and mass in galaxies with varying bulge-to-total mass ratios, finding that the relation is similar across different ratios. This suggests that bulge growth does not significantly affect the star formation rate and mass relation. We also explore the connection between the star formation rate and stellar mass in galaxies with varying specific star formation rates, finding that the relation is similar across different ratios. This indicates that galaxies with varying bulge-to-total mass ratios do not have distinct star formation histories. We conclude that the flattening of the star formation main sequence is primarily caused by the rapid growth of massive galaxies through mergers, rather than bulge growth.

Menger proposed a generalization of the concept of similarity between triangles, defining a relation between three points in a metric space. This relation, which is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, is called a "triangle" if the sum of distances between three points meets a specific condition. Menger's conjecture suggested that in a Euclidean space, a set of points satisfying this condition would also satisfy a similar condition. This conjecture was proven by J. von Neumann in 1936, but the proof was complex and relied on the theory of Hilbert spaces. A simpler proof of this result was later provided by P. P. Erdős in 1946, but it required the use of the theory of inner product spaces. A new proof of this result is presented here, which uses only the theory of metric spaces, demonstrating that a set of points satisfying the initial condition also satisfies a similar condition.

As the size of datasets grows, the computational demands of training models increase, leading to longer training times and higher communication costs. To address these issues, we propose a novel approach called Federated Learning with Local Model Averaging (FLMA), which involves multiple rounds of local model updates before sharing the updated model with a central server. By increasing the number of local updates, we can achieve better model performance with less communication between clients and the server. To evaluate the effectiveness of FLMA, we conduct a theoretical analysis of its convergence rate, demonstrating that the FLMA method can achieve the same convergence rate as traditional federated learning with a single local update, but with a reduced communication cost. We also perform a series of experiments on various datasets, including MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-10, to compare the performance of FLMA with other federated learning methods. Our results show that increasing the number of local updates can significantly improve model accuracy, with minimal communication costs.
